title: The Four German Cases (Die vier Fälle)
summary: German uses four grammatical cases to indicate the role of each noun in a sentence: Nominativ (Subject), Akkusativ (Direct Object), Dativ (Indirect Object / Beneficiary), and Genitiv (Possession / Relation).

tables.title: Definite Articles (Bestimmte Artikel: the)
tables.description: Notice how masculine changes in every single case (der → den → dem → des). Feminine and plural share '-er' in dative/genitive.

tables.title: Indefinite Articles (Unbestimmte Artikel: a / an)
tables.description: There is no plural form for 'ein'. Use 'keine' or zero-article for plural.

tables.title: Personal Pronouns across Cases (Personalpronomen)
tables.description: Personal pronouns replace specific nouns and change form according to case.
rows: you all / to you all (informal pl.)

rules.name: Case Trigger Hierarchy
rules.explanation: Case is assigned in a strict priority: 1) Preposition (overrules everything), 2) Verb governing (e.g. danken + Dativ), 3) Syntactic function (Subject = Nominativ, Direct Object = Akkusativ).

examples.breakdown: sehen takes an accusative direct object → der Mann becomes den Mann
helfen is a dative verb → der Mann becomes dem Mann
The preposition 'mit' strictly demands Dative, regardless of the verb
